harvard_reference: Platt, J.C. (2000) 'Probabilities for SV machines', in Smola, A.J., Bartlett, P., Schölkopf, B. and Schuurmans, D. (eds) Advances in Large-Margin Classifiers. Cambridge, MA: The MIT Press, pp. 61–74. doi:10.7551/mitpress/1113.003.0008.
title: Probabilities for SV Machines
venue: Advances in Large-Margin Classifiers (edited book, eds A.J. Smola, P. Bartlett, B. Schölkopf and D. Schuurmans), The MIT Press
abstract_summary: Platt argues that a classifier's output should be a calibrated posterior probability so that it can be post-processed (e.g. combined with other classifiers or used with asymmetric costs), but standard SVMs give only an uncalibrated decision value. One alternative is to train a kernel classifier directly with a logit link and a regularised maximum-likelihood objective, but that produces non-sparse kernel machines. Platt instead trains an ordinary SVM and then fits the two parameters (A, B) of an additional sigmoid, P(y=1|f) = 1/(1+exp(Af+B)), that maps the SVM output f to a probability; A and B are fitted by maximum likelihood (minimising cross-entropy) on held-out or cross-validated SVM outputs, with a Laplace-style smoothing of the targets to limit over-fitting. Classification error rate and likelihood scores of SVM+sigmoid are compared against a regularised-likelihood kernel machine on three data-mining-style datasets (Reuters, Adult, Web). The SVM+sigmoid produces probabilities of comparable quality to the regularised-likelihood method while retaining the sparseness of the SVM. Published chapter sections: Introduction; Fitting a Sigmoid After the SVM; Empirical Tests; Conclusions; Appendix: Pseudo-code for Training Sigmoid.

claims_supported.claim: Platt scaling fits a sigmoid to classifier scores to produce calibrated probabilities.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (preprint text via OpenAlex W1618905105): 'The output of a classifier should be a calibrated posterior probability ... Standard SVMs do not provide such probabilities ... we train an SVM, then train the parameters of an additional sigmoid function to map the SVM outputs into probabilities.' The published chapter's Section 2 is titled 'Fitting a Sigmoid After the SVM' and its appendix gives pseudo-code for training the sigmoid (section list from OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar records of DOI 10.7551/mitpress/1113.003.0008). The sigmoid form P(y=1|f) = 1/(1+exp(Af+B)) with A, B fitted by maximum likelihood is confirmed by scikit-learn's calibration guide (which cites section 2.1 of Platt 1999) and by a Cornell CS678 (2007) lecture summary of the paper. Caveat: Platt's own text describes fitting the sigmoid to SVM decision values; the name 'Platt scaling' and its application to the scores of arbitrary classifiers are later usage (e.g. Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana, 2005), so the report should not attribute the general term or a claim of generality to this source.

verification_notes: The lead is imprecise. Two versions of this work exist. (1) A 1999 preprint/technical report from Microsoft Research titled 'Probabilistic Outputs for Support Vector Machines and Comparisons to Regularized Likelihood Methods' (OpenAlex W1618905105; primary location CiteSeerX, raw source research.microsoft.com/~jplatt/SVMprob.ps.gz; no DOI; 4,852 OpenAlex citations). This is the form scikit-learn's calibration documentation cites as '[4] J. Platt, 1999' and links to www.cs.colorado.edu/~mozer/Teaching/syllabi/6622/papers/Platt1999.pdf. (2) The published book chapter, retitled 'Probabilities for SV Machines', in Smola, Bartlett, Schölkopf and Schuurmans (eds) Advances in Large-Margin Classifiers, The MIT Press, published 29 September 2000, pp. 61-74, DOI 10.7551/mitpress/1113.003.0008, e-book ISBN 9780262283977 (Crossref record; the edited book itself is Crossref DOI 10.7551/mitpress/1113.001.0001; print ISBN 9780262194488 and 422 pages per MIT Press/Amazon/Waterstones search results). OpenAlex records the chapter with 1,112 citations; Semantic Scholar (CorpusId 64295966) records it with the abstract elided by the publisher and, erroneously, the book editors listed as authors. The Harvard reference above uses the published, DOI-bearing chapter (year 2000, not 1999). Fields not verifiable: volume/issue (none; book chapter). Place of publication 'Cambridge, MA' is The MIT Press's imprint location and is not stated in the Crossref record. Not reachable during verification: mitpress.mit.edu and direct.mit.edu (HTTP 403 to automated fetch), Microsoft Research publication page (404), Google Books API (429), Open Library (fetch quota exhausted). The paper's full text could not be read directly: the Cornell copy fetched (cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs678/2007sp/platt.pdf) is a 2007 lecture presentation summarising the paper, not the paper itself; claim assessment therefore rests on the abstract, the chapter section titles, scikit-learn's description, and that summary. If the report prefers to cite the form used by scikit-learn, an acceptable alternative is: Platt, J.C. (1999) Probabilistic outputs for support vector machines and comparisons to regularized likelihood methods. Preprint. Microsoft Research. Available at: https://www.cs.colorado.edu/~mozer/Teaching/syllabi/6622/papers/Platt1999.pdf (Accessed: 27 September 2026).
caveats: Cite as 2000 (published chapter) rather than 1999 unless deliberately citing the preprint; the chapter title differs from the preprint title. The evidence in the paper is limited to SVMs (linear and quadratic kernels) on three datasets (Reuters, Adult, Web); scikit-learn notes the sigmoid assumption was justified for SVMs in Platt's section 2.1 but 'does not necessarily hold in general', and that the logistic model works best when calibration error is symmetric, which can be a problem for imbalanced problems such as churn. Lin, Lin and Weng (2007, Machine Learning, 68(3), pp. 267-276, doi:10.1007/s10994-007-5018-6) report numerical problems in Platt's original pseudo-code and give a corrected algorithm (the one scikit-learn implements).
